analysis.one_liner: Adds cost-benefit mandates, hearings, and court-review hurdles for major federal regulations.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor in June 2021, the bill sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee with no hearing or vote until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the basic procedures federal agencies must follow to issue major rules — the regulations that set limits on air and water pollution, workplace hazards, financial products, and food and drug safety. It would force agencies to clear extra steps: pre-approval from the White House budget office's regulatory desk, longer comment periods, formal hearings with cross-examination for the biggest rules, a mandate to adopt whichever option 'maximizes net benefits,' and easier court challenges by parties who oppose a rule. Supporters present this as transparency and discipline; each added step also gives regulated companies more openings to delay, dilute, or kill protections before they take effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by federal agencies — energy, manufacturing, chemical, financial, and other firms facing compliance costs — gain the most, because every new procedural step and easier judicial review makes costly rules slower to issue, weaker, or easier to overturn in court. Companies and trade groups with the legal staff to run hearings and lawsuits can use these tools best.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated companies and trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to notify a new White House review process and publish an initiation notice at least 90 days before even proposing a major or high-impact rule, and cannot publish the proposal until that review concludes.

For rules with $100 million or more in annual economic effects, agencies must adopt the alternative that 'maximizes net benefits' — generally the cheapest option — unless a new White House administrator approves a different choice.

For 'high-impact' rules with $500 million or more in annual effects, any interested party could petition for a formal public hearing with oral testimony and cross-examination, with the burden of proof on the agency proposing the rule.

The bill expands judicial review: courts would judge the factual findings behind high-impact rules against a 'substantial evidence' standard, and agencies' interpretations of their own rules would get less deference, giving rule opponents more ways to win in court.

Agencies would face longer comment periods (90 days for major rules), a required 30-day reply window, public dockets for all supporting studies, and periodic published assessments of whether major rules should be modified or repealed.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal safeguards — cleaner air and water, safer workplaces, safer food, drugs, vehicles, and consumer financial products — would bear the cost as protections take longer to issue, tilt toward cheaper weaker versions, or get struck down more easily in court. Emergency and consumer-protection agencies would also spend more staff time on paperwork rather than enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The stack of added steps — 90-day advance notices, mandatory White House sign-off before publication, longer comment windows, and hearing petitions — would slow every major rule, delaying protections for the public even when the underlying law is clear.

The requirement to adopt the option that 'maximizes net benefits' pushes agencies toward the least expensive alternative; benefits that resist dollar calculation, like avoided deaths or illnesses, are hardest to quantify and thus easiest to discount, though the bill does allow unquantified civil-rights and constitutional benefits with special approval.

Formal hearings with cross-examination and expanded court challenges favor parties with large legal budgets; a well-resourced company can use them far more effectively than ordinary citizens or public-interest groups, so the procedural rights are unequal in practice.

A fair supporter's point: the bill would also create real public value, including open dockets for the science behind rules, longer comment periods, a chance to respond to other commenters, and periodic honest reviews of whether major rules still work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and review provisions are genuine improvements, and cost-benefit discipline has legitimate defenders. But the bill's most consequential changes — the net-benefits mandate, mandatory formal hearings, and broader court review — all operate as points of leverage for parties trying to weaken or defeat a rule, and those parties are overwhelmingly large regulated companies. The benefits are procedural; the costs are slower, weaker, more litigated protections for the public. Weighing them honestly, the design trades real public protections for process benefits that mostly accrue to those already best equipped to use the process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rob Portman introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, with one Republican cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs that same day.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — was ever recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Americans who rely on federal health, safety, and financial protections came out ahead, because the existing rulemaking process stayed unchanged and no new barriers were added; regulated industries, meanwhile, did not get the lighter process they sought but also remain subject to the existing rules as written.

for.name: Sen. Rob Portman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not act on it further after referral.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no voting pattern exists; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee and Senate took no action.

industries.industry: Large regulated companies (energy, manufacturing, chemical, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill's added procedural steps, formal hearing rights, and expanded court review primarily benefit firms trying to delay or defeat costly federal rules. Those firms' gain is the public's cost: slower, weaker, more litigated protections.

Small firms face the same federal rules and could formally use the new comment and hearing rights, but without large legal budgets they are far less able to exploit them than big companies, so most of the process would work to the advantage of whoever can afford counsel.
More mandatory analyses, hearings, docket requirements, and litigation means more billable work; the industry gains revenue regardless of whether the public gains protection.
